annotationRationale: The common geometric deduction is that the centroid condition makes ABD equilateral. The shifted-sine and coordinate inequality techniques are alternative optimization routes and remain in their own method mappings.

classificationReview.areaRationale: The problem concerns centroid geometry and the maximum area of a convex quadrilateral, so Geometry replaces Unclassified.
classificationReview.areaCheck: Geometry correctly replaces Unclassified because the problem concerns centroid geometry and an attainable maximum quadrilateral area.

review.questionCheck: Independently, the centroid differences force ABD to be equilateral. The area becomes \(10\sqrt3+12\sin(\theta-60^\circ)\), attaining \(12+10\sqrt3\) at theta = 150 degrees in a convex configuration. Choice C and the key agree; there is no question figure or contradiction.
review.alternativeMethodCheck: LIVE's centroid-difference and trigonometric bound is retained. Random Math's first vector and third complex-number solutions merge into that equivalent route. Its second solution's centroid scaling and Cauchy-Schwarz bound are retained in the coordinate method, replacing Heron's calculation. A separate Heron version adds little learner benefit. No shared-bank methods were supplied.
review.annotationCheck: Centroid ratios and equilateral-triangle recognition are appropriate common assessed concepts, with composite area as support. Optimization techniques remain method-specific, and both retained methods independently prove attainability. Source IDs and third-party classifications are appropriate.
review.areaCheck: Geometry correctly replaces Unclassified because the problem concerns centroid geometry and an attainable maximum quadrilateral area.

methodReviews.mathCheck: All three centroid differences are correct and imply AB = AD = BD. The cosine-law and triangle-area expressions give the stated shifted sine, bounded above by 1. At theta = 150 degrees, the remaining BCD angles sum to 30 degrees; adding the equilateral triangle's 60-degree angles verifies convexity at B and D. The centroid condition also holds for that construction.
methodReviews.sourceMethodCheck: Both cited references support the claimed centroid reduction and trigonometric optimization. The prose adds motivation and a concrete convexity check, with no unsupported official-source claim.
methodReviews.pedagogyCheck: The averaging interpretation, cancellation, area decomposition and equality construction are explained. The shifted-sine step is a direct application of the mapped subtraction identity.
methodReviews.directNodeCheck: All seven IDs are relevant: centroid ratios justify averaging, equilateral properties determine ABD, composite area combines the triangles, and cosine law, sine area, subtraction identity and sine range supply the bound.

nativeLayerJudgments.CN: Accepted CN links support equilateral properties, composite area, sine subtraction and sine range. The supplied centroid, general cosine-law and sine-area nodes have no accepted CN links.
nativeLayerJudgments.US: G-CO.C.10 and G-SRT.D.10/.11 provide partial overlap. F-TF.C.9 is exercised only through one identity. G-SRT.D.9 concerns deriving the sine-area formula, which is only briefly motivated here; graphing and periodicity links are not directly assessed.
nativeLayerJudgments.ailleo: The immediate nodes cover the actual reduction and optimization. Formula application here should not be read as demonstrating every derivation criterion of the sine-area node.

methodReviews.mathCheck: Scaling the centroid pairs about their shared-side midpoints correctly gives all three side equalities. The coordinate constraint and distance formula yield area 10sqrt(3) + v - sqrt(3)u. The square inequality follows from the explicitly displayed nonnegative remainder. Equality at (-3sqrt(3),3) satisfies the circle constraint and produces the verified convex 150-degree configuration.
methodReviews.sourceMethodCheck: Random Math's second solution supports centroid scaling and the Cauchy-Schwarz bound. Replacing Heron with coordinates is honestly identified and independently justified. The exposition is original and correctly classified as third-party-informed.
methodReviews.pedagogyCheck: The scaling construction is explained at use, and the unfamiliar inequality is proved by a square identity. The equality point and convexity argument establish an actual maximum.
methodReviews.directNodeCheck: Every ID is used: centroid ratios and homothety yield the equilateral triangle; distance, triangle area and composite area produce the objective; Cauchy-Schwarz bounds it; the special right-triangle ratio identifies the equality angle.
